summary: By K. Gopalakrishnan From pioneering screen printing technologies to leading the digital printing revolution, Fujifilm Sericol India continues to shape the future of textile printing through innovation, sustainability and customer-centric… The post Beyond Inks: How Fujifilm Sericol is Redefining Sustainable Textile Printing Through Innovation appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: By K. Gopalakrishnan From pioneering screen printing technologies to leading the digital printing revolution, Fujifilm Sericol India continues to shape the future of textile printing through innovation, sustainability and customer-centric solutions The textile printing industry has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past two decades. Once dominated by conventional screen printing, the industry today is rapidly embracing digital technologies, sustainable chemistries, shorter production cycles and increasingly stringent environmental regulations. Global brands are demanding not only superior print quality but also safer chemicals, lower environmental footprints, greater production flexibility and complete compliance with international sustainability standards. Dr. Raghav Rao, Managing Director, Fujifilm Sericol India Pvt. Ltd. At the heart of this transformation, inks have evolved from being merely consumables to becoming strategic enablers of innovation. Whether it is direct-to-garment (DTG), direct-to-film (DTF), sublimation, pigment or reactive printing, the chemistry behind inks today plays a defining role in determining print performance, durability, sustainability and production efficiency. As the textile printing industry continues to evolve, Fujifilm Sericol India Pvt. Ltd. has consistently remained at the forefront of this transformation. Backed by Fujifilm’s global technological leadership and Sericol’s rich heritage in printing inks, the company has spent more than 25 years helping India’s textile printers embrace new technologies while continuously introducing innovations that address the evolving needs of brands, manufacturers and consumers alike. title: Successful Entry into the Coarse-Count Segment with Rieter’s Autoconer X6
title_ko: Rieter의 Autoconer X6으로 Coarse-Count 세그먼트에 성공적으로 진출
summary: To strengthen its market position and diversify beyond commodity yarns, the company Coarser Spinning invested in an integrated Rieter ring spinning and winding solution for yarn counts Ne 4 to… The post Successful Entry into the Coarse-Count Segment with Rieter’s Autoconer X6 appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: To strengthen its market position and diversify beyond commodity yarns, the company Coarser Spinning invested in an integrated Rieter ring spinning and winding solution for yarn counts Ne 4 to Ne 16. The combination of ring spinning machines G 38 and Autoconer X6 winding technology enables efficient coarse-count yarn production with outstanding quality, productivity and cost efficiency. Dharmesh Patel confirms that Autoconer X6 delivers the stability and process control needed for coarse-count spinning Phenix Spinning Pvt. Ltd. founded Coarser Spinning Pvt. Ltd. in 2022 to diversify beyond the highly competitive commodity yarn market. The coarse count segment with yarn counts of Ne 4 to Ne 16 offered opportunities for differentiation and entry into more specialized applications. To succeed, the company needed a reliable and cost-efficient spinning solution capable of producing these coarse yarns with consistent quality at superior productivity. High yarn, splice and package quality were essential to support efficient downstream processing and the company’s long-term growth strategy. Building a future-ready spinning system Coarser Spinning expanded its coarse count production by investing in 10 ring spinning machines G 38 directly linked to the winding machines Autoconer X6 Type V (Fig. 1), creating an integrated Rieter spinning system. With the direct-link setup Coarser Spinning benefits from smooth material flow, high productivity and consistent yarn quality, while minimizing operator intervention. Supported by advanced winding technology, the system delivers excellent yarn, splice and package quality, providing the performance and reliability needed to establish Coarser Spinning in this market segment. content: In a market where sustainability is fast becoming a business priority, SED’s Jodhpur conclave placed industrial water management firmly in the spotlight. As Rajasthan’s manufacturing sector faces tighter environmental norms, sustainable wastewater management has moved from compliance to competitive necessity. Against this backdrop, SED’s ZLD Jodhpur Conclave 2026 brought together industry leaders, technology experts, environmental professionals, and media for a focused discussion on the future of Zero Liquid Discharge solutions. Mr. Vimarsh Verma, Director, SED The conclave was more than a technology showcase. It created a sharp forum for dialogue on how innovation can strengthen environmental performance and operational efficiency. Strong participation from the textile, steel, and wider manufacturing sectors underscored the rising demand for practical, scalable, energy-efficient ZLD technologies. Why Jodhpur Conclave 2026 Matters for Rajasthan’s Textile Industry The conclave comes at a defining moment for Rajasthan’s textile industry. As water scarcity intensifies and compliance costs rise, efficient Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) is no longer optional; it is essential for sustainable and competitive manufacturing. The event brings industry leaders together to explore practical technologies that deliver environmental compliance without compromising commercial viability. Leadership, Innovation and Industry Dialogue Take Centre Stage One of the conclave’s strongest features was its direct, highly interactive format, which brought manufacturers, consultants, environmental professionals and media representatives into conversation with SED’s leadership and engineering team. title: Don’t Stop at Fibre: The Untapped Value in Textile Recycling Wastewater
title_ko: 섬유에서 멈추지 마세요: 섬유 재활용 폐수의 미개척 가치
summary: What if the real value in textile recycling isn’t just in the fibre you recover, but also in the wastewater that can be turned into a valuable resource? Textile recycling… The post Don’t Stop at Fibre: The Untapped Value in Textile Recycling Wastewater appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: What if the real value in textile recycling isn’t just in the fibre you recover, but also in the wastewater that can be turned into a valuable resource? Textile recycling is becoming an increasingly important part of the circular fashion conversation. Old garments are being turned into new yarn. Production waste is becoming feedstock. Fibres are getting another life. But there is an uncomfortable question the industry must ask: what happens to the water used to make that circularity possible? If recycling recovers fibre but leaves behind wastewater loaded with dyes, salts, chemicals and dissolved contaminants, the loop is not truly closed. It simply shifts waste from solid to liquid form. This is the blind spot the industry can no longer ignore. The Global Sustainability Benchmark Is Moving For textile manufacturers targeting international brands, sustainability is no longer a choice; it is a make-or-break factor. It decides who enters global supply chains and who is left behind. The Global Recycled Standard (GRS) requires 20% recycled content for certification and 50% for consumer claims , while also assessing chemical use, environmental systems, chain of custody, and social compliance. However, recycled content alone is insufficient, as broader expectations include water and resource management. Sustainability is now a baseline, not an add-on, defining long-term global competitiveness. The Hidden Water Economy Powering Circularity Textile recycling generates complex wastewater with high TDS, COD, salts, colour, hardness and chlorides. Conventional treatment focuses on safe discharge, but circular manufacturing asks: what value remains in this wastewater? title: Ester Industries Charts a New Course for Textile Circularity with Groundbreaking Loop Industries Joint Venture
summary: By K. Gopalakrishnan ₹1,000 crore plus investment aims to establish India’s first large-scale textile-to-textile chemical recycling facility, positioning the country at the forefront of the global circular economy The global… The post Ester Industries Charts a New Course for Textile Circularity with Groundbreaking Loop Industries Joint Venture appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: By K. Gopalakrishnan ₹1,000 crore plus investment aims to establish India’s first large-scale textile-to-textile chemical recycling facility, positioning the country at the forefront of the global circular economy The global textile industry has long grappled with one of its biggest sustainability challenges, what to do with the millions of tonnes of polyester textile waste generated every year. While PET bottle recycling has evolved into a mature industry, recycling post-consumer polyester textiles, especially coloured fabrics and blended materials, has remained a complex technological hurdle. Conventional recycling technologies have struggled to process real-world textile waste efficiently, leaving a significant gap in achieving true circularity. Ester Industries Ltd. believes it has found the solution. Mr. Vaibhav Jha, CEO, Ester Industries Ltd Through its ₹1,000 crore joint venture with Canada’s Loop Industries, the company is preparing to establish what is expected to be one of the world’s first large-scale commercial facilities capable of converting real-world polyester textile waste into virgin-quality polyester. More importantly, the technology promises true infinite recyclability, enabling polyester to be recycled repeatedly without degradation in quality. Speaking to The Textile Magazine, Mr. Vaibhav Jha, CEO, Ester Industries Ltd., explains how this ambitious venture could reshape the future of polyester recycling while placing India firmly on the global sustainability map. summary: Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE) organized a technical training under its Partnership for Implementation of Innovation Circles (PIIC) initiative on “Sustainable Dye House: Improving RFT, Reducing Re...
content: Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE) organized a technical training under its Partnership for Implementation of Innovation Circles (PIIC) initiative on “Sustainable Dye House: Improving RFT, Reducing Reprocessing and Lowering Water and Steam Consumption” on 23 August at the House of Textile Today in Dhaka. The training brought together professionals from Hams Group, Arien Knit Composite Ltd., Auko-Tex Group and Mondol Group, among the 16 factories participating in PIIC Season 1. Participants included dyeing laboratory and production professionals as well as GM, AGM and Assistant Manager-level representatives involved in knit dyeing operations. Figure : Technical training on Sustainable Dyehouse by TIE. The session was conducted by Rahat Ullah Rashed, Head of Technical Support, Taiwan Persotex Corporation, who has nearly 20 years of experience in the knit dyeing industry. A major focus of the training was improving Right First Time (RFT) performance to reduce reprocessing, which directly contributes to lower water, energy and chemical consumption. The session discussed laboratory preparation, lab-to-bulk correlation and bulk-to-bulk RFT, including practical limitations of laboratory dyeing compared with bulk production. Participants also explored dye combination selection, cotton dyeing techniques and differences in developing light and dark shades in bulk production. Another key area was resource efficiency. The trainer discussed opportunities for bath reduction, lower-temperature pretreatment, optimized hot washing, wash-off and rinsing. Reducing unnecessary baths can lower both water and steam consumption, supporting more efficient dye-house operations. content: The BUTEX Business Club, a prominent student organization of Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX), has announced its 12-member executive committee for the 2026–27 session. Tousif Ishraq, Vice President (Operations); Meherin Sultana, Vice President (Public Relations); Hasanat Touhidul Rahman, Vice President (Creative Affairs); Fariha Yasmin, Vice President (Events); Md. Tanvirul Islam, Vice President (Communications); Md. Ejaz Ahmed, Vice President (Logistics & Finance); and Md. Mahdi Hasan Chowdhury, Vice President (Media & Publications). Rakibul Islam will also oversee the Vice President (IT) portfolio. Speaking after taking charge, President Md. title: Calculating The Cost Of A Prompt
summary: Two brand co-founders wrestle with why, whether, and where to deploy generative AI, stacking potential efficiency gains against environment and ethics. The post Calculating The Cost Of A Prompt appeared first on The Interline .
content: This article was originally released in The Interline’s AI Report 2026 . Including profiles and exclusive interviews with 17 AI companies, stories and opinions from 12 different industry perspectives, and real survey feedback from around 100 voices from every level of fashion, bottled and analysed, The AI Report 2026 is essential reading for anyone interested in AI for fashion. When you’re building a new company in the AI era, it seems like it would be second nature to introduce Generative AI workflows. We hear so much about “AI native” businesses being inevitable that we’ve all but forgotten that some companies might want to choose a different path, and that plenty more find themselves torn over whether the possibilities of AI are worth the potential trade-offs. It’s not just entrenched companies that think this way, either. We’re building a forward-thinking, tech-first, data-native fashion brand, and we hit an important early stage in our journey where we collectively decided we needed to pause, put down the prompts, and reflect on AI’s relationship with people, planet, and production, before we pushed blindly ahead. And sustainability was also just one of the concerns that made us stop and reflect. In an industry that has become reliant on fast-paced, automated systems, is defined by overproduction and overconsumption, and is now rushing headlong towards agentic decision-making, we found ourselves questioning what work can be done by AI, and what work should remain human-centric. title: AMFB expands Executive Board to 21 members, announces policy initiatives for Bangladesh’s apparel industry
summary: The Apparel Merchandiser Foundation of Bangladesh (AMFB) has announced an expanded Executive Committee comprising 21 executive board members, aiming to strengthen its organizational capacity and play...
content: The Apparel Merchandiser Foundation of Bangladesh (AMFB) has announced an expanded Executive Committee comprising 21 executive board members, aiming to strengthen its organizational capacity and play a more effective role in addressing the emerging challenges of Bangladesh’s Ready-Made Garment (RMG) and apparel industry. Figure: AMFB expands Executive Board to 21 members, announces policy initiatives for Bangladesh’s apparel industry. The announcement was made today at a grand discussion and industry dialogue held at Uttara Club, Dhaka, organized by AMFB to discuss the recent crises and emerging challenges facing the RMG sector, particularly issues affecting the apparel merchandising community and the broader industry. Industry professionals, apparel merchandisers, and stakeholders participated in the program, where participants emphasized the need for stronger collaboration, practical policy initiatives, and greater representation of merchandising professionals in industry-level discussions. Focus on policy recommendations During the discussion, AMFB identified several contemporary challenges confronting the apparel and merchandising sector and agreed to develop a set of policy recommendations and strategic proposals. These recommendations will subsequently be presented for further discussion with relevant policymakers, industry leaders, factory owners and other stakeholders. AMFB believes that apparel merchandisers play a critical role in Bangladesh's export-oriented RMG industry, connecting international buyers, manufacturers and supply-chain stakeholders. Therefore, strengthening the professional community is essential for improving competitiveness, productivity, communication and the long-term sustainability of the sector. content: A.T.E. Enterprises Private Limited has appointed Abhijit A Kulkarni as a member of its Board of Directors and designated him Director – Textile Engineering Group (TEG), TeraSpin and HMX. The appointment recognises Mr Kulkarni’s significant contribution to the company and the Board’s confidence in his leadership. Mr Kulkarni has played a key role in strengthening the company’s TEG and TeraSpin businesses and is playing a leading role in the transformation of its HMX business. His customer-centric approach, technical expertise, extensive experience, clear thinking and commitment to operational excellence have helped shape strategies and action plans that support the achievement of the company’s goals. He has consistently demonstrated his ability to build capable teams, foster innovation and support sustainable business performance. His appointment to the Board reflects the increasing responsibilities he has assumed over the past five years and represents the next step in his leadership journey. The Board of Directors congratulates Mr Kulkarni on his appointment and looks forward to his continued contribution to the growth and success of A.T.E. Enterprises Private Limited. title: boltt Reinforces Consumer Trust with 3+4 Software Commitment
summary: Evo and Ace to receive 3 major Android OS upgrades and 4 years of security updates, with security updates delivered at least once every quarter As software support becomes an increasingly important part of the smartphone ownership experience, boltt is strengthening its commitment to long-term device support by introducing its boltt 3+4 Software Commitment for […] The post boltt Reinforces Consumer Trust with 3+4 Software Commitment appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: Evo and Ace to receive 3 major Android OS upgrades and 4 years of security updates, with security updates delivered at least once every quarter As software support becomes an increasingly important part of the smartphone ownership experience, boltt is strengthening its commitment to long-term device support by introducing its boltt 3+4 Software Commitment for its Evo and Ace smartphones. Under the commitment, both smartphones will receive three major Android OS upgrades and four years of security updates, with security updates delivered at least once every quarter. Critical security updates will also be released as required, ensuring that important vulnerabilities can be addressed outside the regular update cycle. For consumers, the value of a smartphone increasingly extends beyond its specifications at the time of purchase. With the 3+4 Software Commitment, boltt is putting greater emphasis on what happens after the purchase, helping ensure that its devices remain secure, supported, and relevant through a longer ownership journey. The commitment provides a simple and transparent framework for software support: 3 major Android OS upgrades, helping keep the software experience current across multiple Android generations. 4 years of security updates, providing long-term protection beyond the initial purchase period. A minimum quarterly security update cadence, with additional updates released where required. Critical security updates as needed, allowing important vulnerabilities to be addressed outside the regular update cycle. A clear and transparent support timeline, counted from the official product launch date. The commitment also reflects a broader shift in how consumers evaluate smartphone value. content: Première Vision Paris returns from 1-3 September 2026, bringing together nearly 900 international exhibitors and a broad range of expertise aimed at helping fashion and textile companies address rapidly changing market, technology and sustainability demands. The September edition will place particular emphasis on its Inno-Tech theme, exploring developments reshaping product creation, manufacturing and development processes. Artificial intelligence, advanced materials, digital solutions, automation and technologies supporting more sustainable production will feature prominently. More than 900 international players will present across the show’s eight universes: Yarns, Fabrics, Designs, Accessories, Leather, Manufacturing, Smart Creation and Bag, Shoes & Leatherwear. Innovations will address areas including performance, transparency, traceability and environmental transition. Smart Creation will showcase next-generation materials including leather alternatives produced from food waste, mycelium-derived biomaterials, PLA fibres, closed-loop recycled polyesters and plant-based alternatives to fur. The area will also feature the ten winners and finalists of the 2026 ANDAM Innovation Prize, highlighting start-ups and technologies contributing to the transformation of the fashion industry. Companies presenting solutions include Hyosung, Uncaged Innovations, Dimpora, EverDye, Alterskin, SynMetabio, Peelsphere, Oleago and Sofileta. Traceability, Digital Product Passports and circularity will form another important part of the programme. Technologies will demonstrate how companies can monitor raw materials, manage certifications, improve supply chain visibility and create value from deadstock. © Première Vision Lenzing, Arvind Limited, Ipeker, A. content: By MK Prabhakar SCM Garments is a name that needs little introduction to anyone associated with the Indian textile and apparel industry. Part of the renowned SCM Group and established in 1989, the company has grown into one of India’s leading garment manufacturers, catering to several prominent apparel brands in the US and the UK. At the recently concluded Bharat Tex 2026, the company’s vibrant and thoughtfully designed booth drew significant attention, attracting a steady stream of visitors throughout the exhibition. Mr. Vikram Vinayagam, Executive Director During the event, The Textile Magazine caught up with M. Arul Saravanan, Chief Marketing Officer, who shared insights into the company’s recent performance, expansion plans, experience at Bharat Tex 2026 and its growth roadmap for the coming years. Navigating a Challenging Year Reflecting on the company’s performance during FY 2025-26, Arul Saravanan acknowledged that it had been a demanding year for the textile industry as a whole. “The last financial year was tough sailing, not only for us but for the textile industry in general. Our exports to the US were impacted due to tariff-related uncertainties. However, there were also positive developments in the form of the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with the UK, EU and New Zealand. The US market is also showing signs of recovery,” he said. summary: The global denim industry is going through a noticeable shift. For years, fast fashion dominated wardrobes by offering trendy, affordable jeans that could be replaced every season. But today, consumer...
content: The global denim industry is going through a noticeable shift. For years, fast fashion dominated wardrobes by offering trendy, affordable jeans that could be replaced every season. But today, consumers are starting to think differently. Global Denim Market Snapshot [Sources: Grand View Research denim jeans market report 2025–2030; IMARC premium denim market report 2025–2033.] Why fast fashion denim still matters Fast fashion denim became popular because it made trends affordable and accessible. Retailers developed rapid supply chains that could move a design from concept to store shelves often introduce new collections every 2–6 weeks. Low pricing also attracts younger shoppers and budget-conscious buyers within the $20–60 price range. Fast fashion denim also benefits from impulse buying. Social media platforms influence rapid trend cycles, encouraging customers to purchase the latest styles. Oversized denim, cargo jeans, distressed finishes, and wide-leg silhouettes can become popular within weeks. Premium denim is growing through value The premium denim segment reached nearly $9.9 billion in 2024 and is expected to grow steadily over the next decade. Consumers are increasingly considering cost-per-wear rather than price alone. A premium pair of jeans may cost significantly more, but it often lasts longer, maintains fit, and provides better comfort. Premium denim brands emphasize fabric quality, craftsmanship, and exclusivity. Japanese selvedge denim, handcrafted washing techniques, organic cotton blends, and limited edition collections create higher perceived value. Sustainability is influencing consumer demand The denim industry has long been criticized for high water use, chemical processing, and overproduction.
